claims.claim: Foundation-model access on serving endpoints takes three forms: pay-per-token endpoints, provisioned-throughput endpoints sized in model units with optional burst scaling, and external-model endpoints that forward to a named provider using a key referenced from a secret scope.

MLflow's ResponsesAgent is a base class that wraps agent logic written with any framework for deployment with MLflow, and the Mosaic AI Agent Framework SDK deploys a Unity Catalog agent model version to an agent serving endpoint.

The SDK's agent_bricks service manages Custom LLMs, each with instructions, guidelines, a serving endpoint name and Unity Catalog datasets of request and optional response columns used for training and evaluation, not inference, with an optimization lifecycle from CREATED through COMPLETED, FAILED or CANCELLED.

The Databricks SDK for Python changelog records put_ai_gateway in v0.33.0 (2024-09-26), knowledge_assistants in v0.97.0 (2026-03-09), supervisor_agents in v0.105.0 (2026-04-23), the Unity Catalog ai_gateway service in v0.123.0 (2026-07-30) and ai_functions in v0.134.0 (2026-09-03).

In databricks-agents 1.12.0, deploy() creates or updates an agent endpoint for a Unity Catalog model version with an AI Gateway inference table, sends 100 percent of traffic to the new version while earlier versions stay served at 0 percent, sets a tracing experiment when one is found and otherwise warns that traces will not be logged in real time or monitored, and leaves scale-to-zero off by default.

mlflow.genai.evaluate runs built-in scorers such as Correctness, RetrievalGroundedness, RelevanceToQuery, Safety, Guidelines and ToolCallCorrectness, and custom scorers, over traces, labelled rows or inputs passed to a predict function; Knowledge Assistants and Supervisor Agents each carry an MLflow experiment ID and examples with guidelines.

SDK 0.141.0 lists external-model providers ai21labs, anthropic, amazon-bedrock, cohere, databricks-model-serving, google-cloud-vertex-ai, openai, palm and custom; the Terraform provider v1.133.0 says an endpoint with an external model serves only that entity and cannot later be converted to or from an external model.

Task-specific AI Functions such as ai_classify, ai_extract and ai_parse_document perform one task with a managed model, and ai_query sends each request to a serving endpoint the caller names, including for batch inference over tables.

The serving-endpoint AI Gateway configuration covers rate limits in calls or tokens per minute keyed by endpoint, user, user group or service principal, input and output guardrails (safety, PII with BLOCK, MASK or NONE, keywords and topics), usage tracking in system tables for usage and associated costs, inference tables and fallback; SDK 0.141.0 says external-model, provisioned-throughput and pay-per-token endpoints are fully supported while agent endpoints currently support only inference tables.

The Terraform provider v1.133.0 model serving page says the ai_gateway block supports only external model endpoints as of now, marks invalid_keywords and valid_topics deprecated and says the PII behavior supports only BLOCK, statements narrower than the SDK 0.141.0 docstrings.

A Genie space is set up by analysts so that business users can ask natural-language questions of data registered in Unity Catalog; Genie requires at least CAN USE permission on a Pro or Serverless SQL warehouse.

A Knowledge Assistant is configured with a display name, a description, optional instructions, knowledge sources of type index (a vector search index), files (a Unity Catalog volume path) or file_table (a table with a binary file column) and examples with guidelines; it reports an agent endpoint, an MLflow experiment and a CREATING, ACTIVE or FAILED state; non-index sources are synced and report a knowledge cutoff time, and index sources are not synced by the assistant, so they are as fresh as their index.

Open-source MLflow 3.16.1 ships a gateway server titled MLflow AI Gateway that its operator starts from a configuration file on a chosen host and port; its start command is deprecated in favour of a UI-based AI Gateway in MLflow, and the gateway module includes budget and guardrail code.

Pay-per-token is charged by tokens processed and suits getting started and variable volume; provisioned throughput provides dedicated capacity for production workloads that need predictable performance; availability of models and modes varies by region.

Model Serving endpoints expose models and agents as REST endpoints on Databricks-managed serverless compute that does not appear in the customer's cloud account; an endpoint holds up to ten served entities with traffic routes, and permission levels are CAN_VIEW, CAN_QUERY and CAN_MANAGE.

Terraform provider v1.133.0 pages label the Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent resources Public Beta and the Unity Catalog model service resource GA, each badge linking to the Databricks release-types page, and state that the provisioned-throughput endpoint resource is in private preview and only available for enrolled customers.

A Supervisor Agent routes each request among configured tools whose types include genie_space, knowledge_assistant, uc_function, uc_connection (an external MCP server), uc_mcp, app, volume, dashboard, serving_endpoint, table, vector_search_index, catalog, schema, supervisor_agent, databricks_web_search and skill; it reports a serving endpoint and an MLflow experiment and takes examples with guidelines.

SDK 0.141.0 includes a Unity Catalog AI Gateway API managing model services (governed endpoints routing to pay-per-token, provisioned-throughput or external destinations with fallback, rate limits and an inference table), model provider services and MCP services as securables governed by Unity Catalog privileges; the Terraform provider v1.133.0 labels the model service resource GA.

With AI Gateway usage tracking enabled, system tables record operational usage on endpoints and associated costs; a query's client_request_id is recorded in the inference and usage tracking tables; endpoint tags are propagated to billing logs.

Foundation-model access on Databricks serving endpoints comes as pay-per-token endpoints, provisioned-throughput endpoints sized in model units with optional burst scaling, and external-model endpoints that forward to a named provider using a key referenced from a secret scope.

A Knowledge Assistant is configured with a description, optional instructions, knowledge sources (a vector search index, Unity Catalog volume files or a file table) and examples, and reports an agent endpoint, an MLflow experiment and a state; non-index sources must be synced. A Supervisor Agent routes requests among configured tools such as Knowledge Assistants, Genie spaces, Unity Catalog functions, MCP connections and apps.

AI Gateway usage tracking records operational usage on endpoints and associated costs in system tables and endpoint tags propagate to billing logs; no artifact read states a rate, so rates come from current pricing.
A custom agent wraps its own logic in MLflow's ResponsesAgent interface, which can wrap any agent framework, and is deployed to an agent endpoint with the Mosaic AI Agent Framework SDK.

mlflow.genai.evaluate runs built-in scorers such as Correctness, RetrievalGroundedness, Safety and Guidelines, and custom scorers, over labelled rows, traces or inputs passed to a predict function; Knowledge Assistants carry examples with guidelines and an MLflow experiment.
Task-specific AI Functions such as ai_classify, ai_extract and ai_parse_document perform one task with a managed model, and ai_query sends each row's request to a serving endpoint the caller names.

The serving-endpoint AI Gateway provides rate limits, guardrails, usage tracking in system tables, inference tables and fallback; SDK 0.141.0 says external-model, provisioned-throughput and pay-per-token endpoints are fully supported while agent endpoints currently support only inference tables, and the Terraform provider v1.133.0 page states a narrower, external-only scope.

Pay-per-token is charged by tokens processed and suits getting started and variable volume; provisioned throughput provides dedicated capacity for production workloads that need predictable performance; availability of models and modes varies by region.

Serving endpoints run on Databricks-managed serverless compute outside the customer's cloud account, hold served entities and traffic routes and grant CAN_QUERY to callers; the agent framework's deploy() puts a Unity Catalog agent model version on an agent endpoint with an inference table, keeping earlier versions served at zero traffic.

The Terraform provider v1.133.0 labels the Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent resources Public Beta and states that its provisioned-throughput endpoint resource is in private preview for enrolled customers; these are dated labels on named artifacts, not availability for any workspace, region or cloud.
In Spark 4 spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true by default: invalid input to a SQL operator or function raises an error instead of returning NULL, and try_cast tolerates malformed input by returning NULL.

A TIMESTAMP is an instant normalised to UTC and rendered in the session time zone, which is a configuration parameter defaulting to UTC on Databricks and settable with SET TIME ZONE; date_format zone letters print the offset; a local time inside a daylight-saving gap is moved to the next valid time and an ambiguous local time in a repeated hour takes the earlier offset.

try_cast, try_divide and try_element_at return NULL where CAST, division and element_at raise under ANSI mode; element_at is 1-based; add_months clamps to the shorter month; datediff(end, start) subtracts start from end; timestampdiff and timestampadd take a unit first and timestampdiff counts whole units, truncating the fraction; unix_timestamp returns epoch seconds.
LEFT SEMI JOIN keeps left rows that have at least one match and LEFT ANTI JOIN keeps left rows with none; neither returns right-side columns or repeats a left row per match.

TIMESTAMP_NTZ stores calendar fields without a zone; changing the session time zone changes how TIMESTAMP values render but leaves TIMESTAMP_NTZ and DATE values unchanged; convert_timezone moves an NTZ value between named zones.

A comparison with NULL is unknown and a WHERE keeps only true; NOT IN with a NULL in the list is never true while NOT EXISTS is unaffected; SUM, AVG and COUNT(column) skip NULL and COUNT(*) does not; GROUP BY, DISTINCT and set operators treat NULLs as one group; <=> is null-safe.
Spark sorts NULLs first under ASC and last under DESC unless NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST is written.

QUALIFY filters window-function results in Databricks SQL and Databricks Runtime (the page's Applies-to label states the minimum runtime); it needs a window function in the SELECT list or in the clause itself.

UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT match columns by position, default to DISTINCT and give each result column the least common type of the branch columns; ALL keeps duplicates; INTERSECT has a higher precedence than UNION and EXCEPT.

T-SQL DATEDIFF(datepart, startdate, enddate) counts datepart boundaries crossed; T-SQL ISNULL replaces NULL with a replacement value; T-SQL DATEADD returns the type of its date argument; T-SQL GETDATE returns the current system timestamp; Oracle TRUNC(n1, n2) truncates a number to n2 decimal places.

With ORDER BY and no frame the default window frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes peer rows; ROWS frames count physical rows while RANGE frames bound rows by an offset on the ordering value; rank shares and skips at a tie, dense_rank shares without skipping, row_number never shares.
In Spark 4, spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true by default: invalid input to a SQL operator or function raises an error instead of returning NULL, and try_cast tolerates malformed input by returning NULL.

A TIMESTAMP is an instant rendered in the session time zone; the session zone is a configuration parameter that defaults to UTC on Databricks and can be set with SET TIME ZONE; date_format pattern letters and offsets are documented; a local time inside a daylight-saving gap is moved to the next valid time, and an ambiguous local time in a repeated hour takes the earlier offset.

try_cast, try_divide and try_element_at return NULL where their strict counterparts raise under ANSI mode; element_at indexes are 1-based; add_months, last_day, date_add, datediff(end, start), timestampdiff and timestampadd have the documented signatures, and timestampdiff counts whole units.
LEFT SEMI JOIN returns left rows that have a match and LEFT ANTI JOIN returns left rows with no match; neither adds right-side columns.

Comparisons with NULL yield unknown; NOT IN with a NULL in the list is never true; aggregates other than COUNT(*) skip NULL; GROUP BY, DISTINCT and set operators group NULLs together; <=> is null-safe equality.
The QUALIFY clause filters window-function results in Databricks SQL and Databricks Runtime; the page's Applies-to label gives the minimum runtime version, which must be checked for the target.
UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT match columns by position, default to DISTINCT and coerce column types to a common type; ALL keeps duplicates.

T-SQL DATEDIFF(datepart, startdate, enddate) returns the count of datepart boundaries crossed between start and end; T-SQL ISNULL replaces NULL with a replacement value; T-SQL DATEADD returns the data type of its date argument; Oracle TRUNC(n1, n2) truncates a number to n2 decimal places.

Window functions compute a value per row over a partition ordered by ORDER BY; with ORDER BY and no frame the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes peer rows; ROWS and RANGE frames and the ranking functions RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER are documented.
Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles) are a documented way to define an app and its resources as configuration and deploy it per target.

Deploying an app builds and starts it from its source files: files synced to a workspace folder are deployed through the UI or with databricks apps deploy and a source code path; the deployment installs Python packages from requirements.txt and Node.js packages from package.json, runs a build script when one is defined, and then runs the start command given in app.yaml.
The platform forwards the signed-in user's identity to the app in HTTP request headers, including X-Forwarded-Email and X-Forwarded-User, which the back end reads per request.

Adding a Lakebase database as an app resource gives the app's service principal a matching Postgres role named after its client ID, grants CONNECT and CREATE on the chosen database and injects connection details such as PGHOST as environment variables; privileges on tables the app did not create are granted separately.

Unity Catalog row filters restrict the rows a query returns and column masks return original or masked values at query time, evaluated for the principal that runs the query, with documented limits on supported access paths.

Databricks Apps hosts data and AI web applications on serverless compute that Databricks provisions and manages, integrated with workspace resources such as SQL warehouses, model serving endpoints and Lakebase databases; the documented frameworks include Streamlit, Dash, Gradio, Flask and FastAPI for Python and React, Angular, Svelte and Express for Node.js, and users reach an app at its URL after signing in.

Each Databricks app has a dedicated service principal, unique to the app and not reusable by another app; Databricks injects its OAuth credentials into the app environment as DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET, and under app authorization every call made with them is evaluated against that principal's permissions, whoever is signed in.

An app's resources, such as a SQL warehouse, a model serving endpoint, a secret or a Lakebase database, are each added with a chosen permission for the app's service principal (for example Can use on a warehouse, Can query on an endpoint) and a resource key that app.yaml maps to an environment variable with valueFrom, so no ID or credential is hard-coded.

User authorization (on-behalf-of-user) forwards the signed-in user's access token to the app in the X-Forwarded-Access-Token header; calls made with it are evaluated with the user's own permissions, bounded by scopes the app declares, such as sql, and access outside approved scopes is blocked even when the user's permissions are broader. An access connector for Azure Databricks is a first-party Azure resource carrying a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity; that identity is granted a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor; a storage credential names the connector's resource ID and an external location binds an abfss path to the credential; a managed identity needs no secret rotation and can reach storage protected by network rules, unlike a service principal; Unity Catalog checks access to the credential or location before authenticating to Azure.

Creating a storage account grants no data access through Entra; data roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor are assigned explicitly at subscription, resource group, account or container scope, and changes can take up to ten minutes to apply.

Public DNS returns a CNAME into a privatelink name that a linked Private DNS zone can answer with a private endpoint's IP; the zones are privatelink.azuredatabricks.net for Azure Databricks, privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net for the ADLS dfs sub-resource and privatelink.blob.core.windows.net for blob; DNS resolution and access control are independent, and a resource with public access disabled rejects connections whatever DNS says.

When a VNet uses a Private DNS zone for a resource type, it resolves public resources of that type only if they have no private endpoint connections; otherwise the zone answers NXDOMAIN unless fallback to internet or another DNS configuration is added.

Serverless egress control applies account-level network policies, one per workspace at a time, that set the network access mode for serverless workloads; account admins manage them from the account console; the workspace must be on the Premium tier; most changes refresh within ten minutes and mode or enforcement changes can take up to 24 hours.

A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP from the VNet; its connection is Approved, Pending, Rejected or Disconnected, only Approved endpoints carry traffic, and a manual request waits for the resource owner's approval; each storage sub-resource needs its own endpoint.

The workspace storage account in the managed resource group holds workspace system data and the DBFS root; enabling its firewall support blocks public access, Databricks reaches it through an access connector it creates, serverless must use service or private endpoints, and the trusted-services setting admits any Azure Databricks access connector in the same tenant.

A Microsoft Entra ID Global Administrator establishes the Databricks account's first account admin; the SCIM provisioning connector cannot sync nested groups or Entra service principals; automatic identity management syncs users, groups, memberships, nested groups and service principals and is documented as enabled by default for accounts created after August 1, 2025.

Azure Databricks customer-managed keys come from Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM for managed disks (classic compute only), managed services (control-plane data) and the DBFS root (not additional mounts); the DBFS root Key Vault needs soft delete and purge protection.

Direct access to ADLS Gen2 outside Unity Catalog uses the abfss driver with an Entra service principal's OAuth credentials, a storage account key or a SAS token; Shared Key grants access to every resource in the account, service and account SAS tokens are signed with the account key, SAS generation cannot be audited, and disallowing Shared Key rejects key-authorized requests while Entra-authorized ones continue.

The Databricks SDK turns an Azure login redirect carrying a private-link-validation-error into PrivateLinkValidationError, a subclass of PermissionDenied whose message says the workspace has Azure Private Link enabled and is not accessible from the current network.

Deny assignments, created and managed by Azure, block resource actions even when a role assignment grants them; Azure Databricks places a system deny assignment on its managed resource group, removed only when the workspace is deleted, so tags belong on the workspace resource.

Storage firewall rules admit traffic to an account's public endpoint by virtual network, IP, resource instance or trusted-service exception; allowed sources must still be authorized; a disallowed subnet receives a 403; a resource instance rule admits the endpoint, not the data, which needs a role for the resource's managed identity; Azure Databricks access connectors are admitted by managed identity.

For API versions released after March 31, 2026, subnets in new virtual networks are private by default, so virtual machines need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway or a route to a firewall; existing virtual networks are unchanged.

Entra security principals that can hold Azure roles are users, groups, application service principals and managed identities; a managed identity's service principal has no application object and cannot be modified directly; a system-assigned identity shares its resource's lifecycle, a user-assigned one has its own.

Azure Databricks supports three independently enabled Private Link types: inbound from users through databricks_ui_api and browser_authentication endpoints in a transit VNet, classic from clusters through a databricks_ui_api endpoint in the workspace VNet, which requires the Premium plan and VNet injection, and outbound from serverless compute; compute must resolve the workspace URL to the endpoint's private IP through privatelink.azuredatabricks.net linked to its VNet or DNS forwarding.

Azure chooses a route by longest prefix match; next hop types include Virtual network, Internet, None and Virtual appliance, and a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a virtual appliance lets it inspect traffic; Internet-bound traffic to Azure services travels the Azure backbone; service tags can be route prefixes, up to 25 such routes per table.

With secure cluster connectivity, classic nodes have no public IP addresses and the VNet has no open ports; each cluster connects outbound on port 443 to the control plane's relay over the Microsoft backbone; it is enabled automatically for portal and ARM deployments; the default VNet gets a NAT gateway from Databricks, while an injected workspace should have a stable egress IP.

Network connectivity configurations are account-level regional objects attached to workspaces; without a private endpoint, serverless reaches Azure storage through service endpoints from stable subnets and other resources from NAT IPs; a private endpoint rule makes Databricks request an endpoint that the resource owner must approve, and it is effective only when ESTABLISHED, expiring if not approved within 14 days; changes usually propagate within ten minutes and can take up to 24 hours.

An injected workspace needs a user-defined route for every type of outbound connection; Databricks recommends service tags over IP addresses; the AzureDatabricks tag covers the control plane, secure cluster connectivity relay and web application, the Storage tag artifact and log Blob storage, and the EventHub tag logging.

VNet injection uses two dedicated subnets, host and container, delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces and not shared with other workspaces or resources, in a /16 to /24 VNet with subnets no smaller than /26; each node takes one address in each subnet and Azure reserves five per subnet; Databricks provisions and manages the required NSG rules through the delegation; a NAT gateway on both subnets is recommended for stable egress.

The dashboard API publishes with embed_credentials; publishing as a service principal needs at least CAN MANAGE on the dashboard, SELECT on its data sources and CAN USE on the warehouse, after which viewers use the principal's permissions and audit logs show the principal as the executor.

AI/BI dashboards keep a best-effort 24-hour result cache: shared across viewers for a dashboard published with shared data permissions, per user for drafts and individual data permissions, and populated by scheduled updates.

AI/BI dashboards are low-code dashboards built from datasets; each dataset is based on a table, view, metric view or custom SQL query, every visualization reads from one or more datasets, and a published dashboard can be shared with users registered to the Databricks account.
Databricks provides ODBC and JDBC drivers for tools and clients; some tools need the ODBC driver installed, such as Tableau Desktop, while recent Power BI Desktop releases include it.

Embedding for external users places a dashboard in an external application for viewers without Databricks accounts, using a service principal with read access to the dashboard and its data and one-hour tokens scoped to each viewer.
A published dashboard stores its field filter and parameter selections in the URL, so a bookmarked or shared link reopens the dashboard with those values applied.

Field filters narrow results by dataset fields and come as single value, multiple values, date picker, date range picker, text entry and range slider; for relatively small datasets they are often applied in the browser without re-running the query.

Genie One, previously Databricks One, is the simplified interface where business users view AI/BI dashboards, ask questions in natural language and use Databricks Apps; the consumer access entitlement directs users there and is the least-privileged option.

A Unity Catalog metric view separates measure definitions from dimensions, is defined in YAML and registered with SQL DDL or Catalog Explorer, lets a query group by any available dimension while the engine generates the computation, and is queried with the MEASURE function.

Dashboard parameters substitute values into dataset queries at runtime so data is filtered before aggregation; parameter filters come as single value, multiple values, date picker and date range, and query-based parameters draw their allowed values from a dataset.

An AI/BI dashboard has its own permission levels, Can View (CAN_READ), Can Run, Can Edit and Can Manage, which govern the dashboard object; whether its queries return data is decided separately by data permissions on the underlying objects.

torch.nn.Embedding is a lookup table storing embeddings of a fixed dictionary and size, returning the vectors for the indices it receives.

A neural network is layers of units that each hold a number, the next layer's numbers computed from the previous layer's; a cost function measures how badly its predictions fit labelled examples, and gradient descent repeatedly moves weights and biases downhill on that cost.

Authentication types include pat (host and token), oauth-m2m for a service principal (host, client ID and client secret), external-browser and databricks-cli for a person's OAuth login, and github-oidc workload identity federation, which needs only the host and client ID.

bundle deploy takes a deployment lock, uploads built libraries and synchronized files, records deployment state and applies a plan; deleting or recreating tracked resources such as schemas, pipelines or volumes needs approval, and a console that cannot prompt fails unless --auto-approve is given.
databricks bundle destroy removes all Databricks resources created by deploying the bundle to a target, after interactive approval or with --auto-approve.

A target in mode: development prefixes resource names with '[dev <short name>] ', tags them dev, pauses schedules and triggers, limits jobs to 4 concurrent runs, marks pipelines as development and disables the deployment lock unless it is enabled.

An include entry without wildcards that matches no file is an error, while a wildcard entry that matches nothing is accepted without any message.

databricks bundle schema generates the JSON Schema that describes bundle configuration for validation and autocomplete, and databricks bundle summary lists the resources a bundle deployed with their workspace URLs.

bundle run starts a deployed job through the Jobs run-now call, waits and reports whether the run was canceled, failed, successful, timed out or skipped, unless --no-wait is given.

Arguments after -- in databricks bundle run are passed to the run, as job parameters when the job uses them; with no resource key, bundle run -- <command> runs a local command with the environment variables that authenticate Databricks tools as the bundle's identity; --no-wait returns without waiting.
A job's run_as names a user, a service principal by application ID, or a group; without it, the job runs as the user who created it.
With the direct deployment engine, databricks bundle plan -o json writes a detailed plan that databricks bundle deploy --plan applies instead of planning again.

The Databricks SDK for Python (Beta) covers the public Databricks REST API, retries requests that are safe to retry, and its authors encourage pinning the exact SDK version because minor releases may contain documented backward-incompatible changes.
Databricks secrets hold credentials for notebooks and jobs instead of pasting them in; displayed secret values are redacted, but a user allowed to read a secret can still read it.

From v1.0.0 the Databricks CLI follows semantic versioning; commands marked Beta or Private Preview and the experimental group may still change in minor releases, and the CLI follows Databricks unified authentication.

Targets override workspace, variables, resources, run_as, presets, permissions, mode and git settings; a target may not assign a variable the root does not declare, and when several targets exist exactly one may be marked default.

The CLI's default Python template lays a project out as src/, resources/, tests/ and fixtures/, declares catalog and schema variables in databricks.yml, and defines a default dev target in development mode and a prod target in production mode with an explicit root_path and a CAN_MANAGE permission.

From CLI v1.0.0, OAuth tokens for interactive logins are stored in the OS-native secure store by default instead of ~/.databricks/token-cache.json; old cached tokens are not migrated, so each profile logs in again, and DATABRICKS_AUTH_STORAGE=plaintext keeps file storage.

bundle validate reports a reference to an undeclared variable as the error 'reference does not exist: ${var.name}', suggests close names, and prints the bundle name, target, workspace user and path in its summary.

A configuration key the bundle schema does not define is reported as the warning 'unknown field: <name>', and the workspace section deliberately has no token, password or client-secret field: those must come from environment variables.

databricks bundle validate checks a target's configuration for errors, warnings and recommendations before deploy, fails on warnings with --strict, and runs an initialize phase that connects to the workspace and reads the current user from the API.

A bundle variable's value comes from --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_<name>, then .databricks/bundle/<target>/variable-overrides.json, then the target's value, then the variable's default; a variable with none of these is an error.

People authenticate with OAuth user-to-machine (databricks auth login); service principals use OAuth machine-to-machine with a client ID and secret, or workload identity federation without a stored secret.
bundle deploy takes a lock, uploads files and built libraries, applies a plan and records state; destructive plans need approval or --auto-approve.
Databricks Git folders are a Git client in the workspace for clone, commit, push, pull and branch changes, used with CI/CD.
Development mode prefixes names with [dev <short name>] and pauses schedules; production mode requires an explicit workspace.root_path unless every job sets run_as or a service principal deploys.
The bundle's workspace section has no token or secret field, and the SDK README advises against hard-coding credentials because they can leak through version control.

Change records include insert, delete, update_preimage and update_postimage labels plus a table commit version; preimage is before and postimage is after the update.
Column mapping supports metadata-only logical renames and drops without rewriting data files; non-additive changes can affect streaming readers and legacy path-based readers.
Optimistic concurrency section separates reading, staging files, and validating a commit; conflict matrix distinguishes ordinary INSERT pairs from overlapping changes.
Deletion vectors record row modifications in metadata and readers apply them when resolving table state; logical removal can precede physical file rewrite.
Introduction and update sections describe Parquet data plus a transaction log, atomic table operations and schema enforcement.
Time-travel retention requires log and data files. RESTORE is a new data-changing operation with downstream duplicate-processing risk.
Reader/writer requirements and feature tables establish that client compatibility depends on enabled table features; an upgrade can exclude older clients.

Liquid clustering is declared with CLUSTER BY, applied incrementally by OPTIMIZE, changeable with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY without rewriting existing data, incompatible with partitioning and ZORDER, limited to four keys with statistics, and adds the clustering and domainMetadata writer features.
DELETE and UPDATE commit new versions; without deletion vectors every file holding a changed row is rewritten whole, and deleted data stays in storage until old versions are vacuumed.
A MERGE can fail when several source rows match the same target row and try to modify it; the source should be preprocessed to one change per key before merging.

Writes are validated against the table schema: DataFrame columns must exist in the table and types must match or the write fails, and table columns missing from the DataFrame are written as null; MERGE UPDATE SET * and INSERT * ignore extra source columns unless automatic schema evolution is enabled.

Columns are added explicitly with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS, for one write with the mergeSchema option, or for a whole session with spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled; added columns are appended; overwriteSchema replaces the schema on overwrite; streams reading the table terminate on a schema change.

Table features are named capabilities in a table's read or write protocol; a client that does not understand a listed feature cannot read or write the table; the change data feed and CHECK constraints are writer features, column mapping and deletion vectors also need readers; protocol upgrades are irreversible.

The change data feed is off by default, is enabled per table with delta.enableChangeDataFeed, records changes only after it is enabled, exposes _change_type values insert, update_preimage, update_postimage and delete with _commit_version, stores UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE changes under _change_data, and follows the table's retention, so VACUUM removes old change files.

VACUUM LITE (Delta 3.3 and above) finds removable files from the transaction log instead of listing the directory and fails with DELTA_CANNOT_VACUUM_LITE when the log has been pruned; the default mode lists the directory and also removes files the table never referenced.

Log entries older than delta.logRetentionDuration (30 days by default) are cleaned up when checkpoints are written, and time travel needs every log entry since the previous checkpoint, so a version inside the file retention can still become unreadable.

MERGE joins a source to a target on a condition; WHEN MATCHED clauses update or delete matched target rows, WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses only insert unmatched source rows, WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clauses update or delete target rows that no source row matches, and a row that no clause selects is left unchanged.

In open-source Delta 3.2 and later, DeltaMergeBuilder.withSchemaEvolution() enables schema evolution for one MERGE without the session-wide autoMerge setting; on Spark 4.0.4 with delta-spark 4.0.0 it added a new source column, while the SQL form MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO added none.

OPTIMIZE compaction coalesces small files into fewer larger ones in a new version without changing data, is idempotent, and leaves readers on snapshot isolation; Z-ordering is not idempotent; auto compaction and optimized writes exist from Delta 3.1.
Databricks supports automatic clustering for managed tables, where clustering keys are set to AUTO and chosen by the platform, alongside keys you choose; clustering keys conflict with partitioning.
Databricks also documents an automatic change data feed for eligible Unity Catalog tables on recent runtimes, distinct from the legacy table property this module enables.

Predictive optimization is a Databricks service for Unity Catalog managed tables that decides when to run maintenance such as OPTIMIZE and VACUUM; it is enabled, disabled or inherited per catalog and schema and is not part of open-source Delta.

On Databricks, which conditions count toward a duplicate match differs between Databricks Runtime 16.0 and above and 15.4 LTS and below, so the runtime is checked before a clause condition is trusted to avoid the error.
Updating a Delta table's schema terminates streams that read the table, which must be restarted, and a change-feed read uses the latest table version's schema.

VACUUM deletes data files that the table no longer references and that were removed longer ago than the retention threshold (7 days by default); it is not automatic in open-source Delta, does not delete log files, ends time travel to versions older than the retention, also removes old change files, and a safety check refuses retentions shorter than the table's; the documentation recommends at least 7 days because concurrent readers and writers may still use old or uncommitted files.
Z-ordering re-clusters all files of a partition on every run and is not idempotent, while bin-packing compaction is idempotent and liquid clustering rewrites only data that needs clustering.

Liquid clustering is declared with CLUSTER BY, applied incrementally by OPTIMIZE, changeable without rewriting data, incompatible with partitioning and ZORDER, and adds writer features; Databricks can also choose keys automatically for managed tables.
DELETE and UPDATE commit new versions; without deletion vectors changed files are rewritten whole, and removed data stays in storage until VACUUM deletes the old files after the retention.
A MERGE fails when several source rows match and try to modify one target row; source rows for keys not yet in the target are each inserted, so the source is de-duplicated before merging.
Enabling a table feature adds it to the table's protocol; writer features bind writers, reader features also bind readers, and protocol upgrades are irreversible.

The change data feed is enabled per table, records changes only after enablement with insert, update_preimage, update_postimage and delete rows, and its change files expire with the table's retention; Databricks also documents an automatic mode for eligible Unity Catalog tables.

OPTIMIZE compacts files without changing rows and is idempotent; VACUUM deletes unreferenced files removed longer ago than the retention (7 days by default), is not automatic in open-source Delta, keeps log files, ends time travel beyond the retention and refuses shorter retentions through a safety check.

MERGE sorts rows into matched (update or delete), not matched (insert only) and not matched by source (update or delete) cases; a row no clause selects is unchanged, and a delete-by-source clause acts only within its condition.

Predictive optimization is a Databricks service for Unity Catalog managed tables that decides when to run maintenance such as OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, set per catalog and schema; open-source Delta has no such scheduler.

Schema enforcement refuses writes with columns the table lacks or mismatched types and fills missing columns with null; evolution adds columns by ALTER TABLE, a per-write mergeSchema option or a session-wide setting, and a schema change stops streams reading the table.
Agent development includes building, evaluation, deployment, tracing, and monitoring; retrieval and tools are distinct responsibilities.
Classic compute runs in the customer AWS account; serverless compute runs in a Databricks-managed plane. Account, workspace, and metastore are distinct constructs.
Classic compute uses networking in the customer AWS account.
Lakeflow Connect offers ingestion tools and connectors, including CDC-based database ingestion.
Cost optimization relates resource decisions to delivered value.

Table features and protocol requirements affect client compatibility.
MLflow supports evaluating traces with code checks and model-based scorers.
Expectations apply record-level Boolean quality constraints and can retain, drop, or fail on invalid data.
Jobs coordinate tasks, dependencies, triggers, and run monitoring.

MERGE can insert, update, and delete; ambiguous multiple source matches need to be resolved.
The platform supports data preparation, training, experiment tracking, model deployment, and monitoring.
Spark Declarative Pipelines supports declarative SQL/Python batch and streaming pipelines; Lakeflow pipelines extend it on Databricks.
Reading a table requires the relevant SELECT and USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA privileges; permissions on objects differ from network reachability.
DataFrames are lazily evaluated; actions cause execution. collect brings results to the driver.
A query profile exposes operators, rows, and resource metrics; viewing needs ownership or suitable warehouse monitoring permission.
Architecture reliability includes recovery and continued operation after failure.
Network connectivity configurations are regional account constructs; resource connectivity depends on location, configuration, and resource type.
Spark SQL and DataFrame interfaces express structured transformations using the same underlying execution engine.

Unity Catalog governs data and AI assets, with catalog.schema.object naming for key assets. Managed and external assets differ in storage lifecycle responsibility.
Warehouse size and cluster count address different capacity dimensions; inspect queues and spills before changing capacity.

pandas merge_asof with direction='backward' selects the last right-hand row whose key is less than or equal to the left key, within groups given by `by`; allow_exact_matches defaults to True; inputs must be sorted by the key.
Databricks primary key, foreign key and unique constraints are informational and not enforced, while Delta Lake enforces CHECK and NOT NULL constraints on new and existing data.
SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True) stacks a MissingIndicator, but a feature with no missing values at fit time gets no indicator even if values are missing at transform time.

A feature table has a primary key and is backed by a Delta table; timestamp keys hold the event time associated with a feature value and, with the primary keys, uniquely identify the value at a point in time; the offline store serves training and batch inference, and a table can be published to an online store for real-time inference.

On-demand features are computed at inference time by Python user-defined functions bound with FeatureFunction in create_training_set and evaluated automatically at inference for models logged with the feature engineering log_model method.

Online Feature Stores, powered by Lakebase, sync offline Unity Catalog feature tables with TRIGGERED (default), CONTINUOUS or SNAPSHOT publish modes; published tables need non-nullable primary keys and Change Data Feed for TRIGGERED and CONTINUOUS; Model Serving automatic feature lookup uses the most recent published values and, for endpoints created from February 2025, can log looked-up values to inference tables; Feature Serving endpoints return feature values to applications; the documentation keeps a migration page for legacy online tables.

A point-in-time lookup with timestamp_lookup_key returns the latest feature values prior to each timestamp for the matching keys, or null; lookback_window excludes older values (default None) during training and batch inference, while online inference always uses the latest value regardless of the lookback window; a time series table has one TimestampType or DateType timestamp key and no partition columns.
Transforms used in training must be applied to test and production data and learnt from training data only; information unavailable at prediction time makes performance estimates overly optimistic.

With RELY, Databricks may use an informational primary key or unique constraint to rewrite queries; ensuring it holds is the user's responsibility and an unsatisfied constraint may yield incorrect results; Photon is required.
Training-serving skew arises from differences in how training and serving pipelines handle data; shared code, one programming language and explicit monitoring of a fraction of traffic reduce it.

Databricks Feature Store registers features in Unity Catalog with governance, lineage, point-in-time joins and online serving; it needs a Unity Catalog-enabled workspace; features are authored as feature tables you populate or as Feature Views that Databricks computes and manages (Public Preview).

Any Delta table in Unity Catalog with a primary key can be a feature table, and a TIMESERIES keyword on a primary key column makes it a time series feature table (Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above).

Feature Views (Public Preview) define features declaratively, including sliding and tumbling time-windowed aggregations, and materialization creates Lakeflow pipelines that populate Unity Catalog tables for training, batch scoring or online serving.
pandas merge_asof with direction='backward' picks the last right-hand row whose key is less than or equal to the left key, within `by` groups, on inputs sorted by the key.
Primary key constraints on Databricks are informational and not enforced; CHECK constraints are enforced by Delta Lake.
Online Feature Stores sync offline Unity Catalog feature tables with TRIGGERED, CONTINUOUS or SNAPSHOT publish modes, and Model Serving can look up the most recent published values automatically.

A point-in-time lookup returns the latest feature values prior to each row's timestamp_lookup_key value, or null; lookback_window excludes older values during training and batch inference, while online inference always uses the latest value.
Training-serving skew comes from differences between how training and serving pipelines handle data; sharing code and monitoring a fraction of traffic reduce it.

Databricks Feature Store registers features in Unity Catalog with lineage, point-in-time joins and online serving; any Delta table in Unity Catalog with a primary key can be a feature table; Feature Views, which Databricks computes and manages, are Public Preview.

system.billing.usage records billable usage with SKU, usage date and time, quantity and unit, custom tags and usage metadata such as job, warehouse and cluster identifiers; corrections arrive as retraction and restatement records beside the original; records arrive after the usage, not instantly.

Budgets monitor account-wide or filtered usage and alert recipients when spending crosses a threshold; the current budget API measures thresholds in list-price US dollars over cumulative monthly spend, shared or per user, and lists email-notification and block-usage action types.

Databricks separates serverless compute, provisioned and scaled on demand, from classic compute the customer configures: all-purpose compute for interactive, shareable and restartable analysis, and job compute that the scheduler creates for a run and terminates afterwards; SQL warehouses are a separate compute type for SQL in serverless, pro or classic form.
The cost optimization pillar groups practice under choosing optimal resources, dynamically allocating resources, monitoring and controlling cost, and designing cost-effective workloads.

An all-purpose cluster terminates after the inactivity minutes set in autotermination_minutes and is not terminated automatically when the field is unset; a SQL warehouse stops after auto_stop_mins idle minutes, which the API defaults to 120, with 0 meaning no auto-stop.

Compute (cluster) policies limit which attributes and values users can set when creating clusters, including limits on attributes that affect the hourly rate; the cost optimization pillar lists compute policies, auto-termination and tagging among its cost controls.

Pools keep idle, ready-to-use instances to reduce cluster start and autoscaling times; Databricks charges no DBUs for instances idle in a pool while the cloud provider's instance billing applies; a SQL warehouse's minimum cluster count keeps clusters running, which may reduce cold starts.

Databricks prices usage pay-as-you-go and defines the DBU as a normalized unit of processing power used for measurement and pricing; the Clusters API maps node instance types to DBUs. This module quotes no rate.

Classic compute can terminate with cloud-side reasons including AWS_RESOURCE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED and AWS_INSUFFICIENT_INSTANCE_CAPACITY_FAILURE; flexible node type settings list alternate node types used as fallbacks when the primary node type is unavailable during launch and upscale.

Custom tags on clusters and SQL warehouses are applied to their cloud resources, such as AWS instances and EBS volumes, alongside default tags, and billable usage rows carry custom tags; serverless usage is attributed through usage policies, formerly budget policies, that carry customer-defined tags, and jobs record the usage policy used for their cost attribution.

Warehouse size and cluster count are different capacity dimensions: a larger size lets larger queries run and the maximum cluster count serves more concurrent queries; serverless warehouses start a query when capacity exists and queue it otherwise; query metrics timestamp waiting for provisioning separately from waiting while the warehouse is at maximum load.

Budgets monitor account-wide or filtered spend and alert recipients at thresholds measured in list-price US dollars per month; the API also lists a block-usage action type.

Serverless compute is provisioned on demand; classic all-purpose compute serves interactive, shareable, restartable work, job compute is created for a run and terminated afterwards, and SQL warehouses serve SQL in serverless, pro or classic form.
All-purpose clusters auto-terminate only when autotermination_minutes is set; SQL warehouses stop after auto_stop_mins idle minutes, which the API defaults to 120.
Pools reduce cluster start and autoscaling times with idle instances; Databricks charges no DBUs for idle pool instances while cloud instance billing applies.
Databricks prices usage pay-as-you-go and defines the DBU as a normalized unit of processing power used for measurement and pricing; no rate is quoted here.

Custom tags on clusters and warehouses reach their cloud resources and the billable usage rows; serverless usage takes tags from usage policies, formerly budget policies.
Databricks documents AutoML as preparing data, training and tuning candidate models, and generating a source notebook for each trial, for classification, regression and forecasting problems.
The naive method forecasts every step as the last observation; the seasonal naive method forecasts each step as the last observed value from the same season.
A prediction interval gives a range within which the future value is expected to lie with a stated probability, under the assumptions of the method that produced it.
Data leakage uses information that would not be available at prediction time when building or evaluating a model, which produces overly optimistic performance estimates.
Scaled errors such as MASE divide forecast errors by the in-sample mean absolute error of a naive or seasonal naive method, giving a unit-free measure that stays defined when actuals are zero.

Percentage errors such as MAPE are infinite or undefined when an actual is zero and extreme when it is close to zero; scikit-learn's mean_absolute_percentage_error divides by the larger of the actual's magnitude and a small epsilon, so a zero actual yields a very large finite value.
The symmetric MAPE still divides by a number close to zero when the actual is close to zero, can be negative in its original form, and is not recommended as a replacement for MAPE.

Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations whose weights decay exponentially as observations get older; seasonal variants such as Holt-Winters add a seasonal component.
A score and the threshold that turns it into an action are separate choices; precision is TP/(TP+FP) and changes with the threshold, which can be set by the costs of the errors it trades.

Time-series cross-validation evaluates forecasts on a rolling forecasting origin: each test set follows its training data in time, and scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit yields successive training sets that are supersets of earlier ones, whereas KFold and ShuffleSplit assume independent samples.

TimeSeriesSplit's test_size sets each test set's length (by default the number of samples divided by n_splits plus one), gap drops samples from the end of each training set before its test set, and max_train_size caps the training window.
Prediction intervals usually widen as the forecast horizon grows, because more uncertainty accumulates the further ahead the forecast reaches.
Databricks documents AutoML as preparing data, training and tuning candidate models and generating a notebook for each trial, for classification, regression and forecasting problems.
The naive method forecasts every step as the last observation; the seasonal naive method forecasts each step as the last observed value from the same season.
A prediction interval states a range expected to contain the future value with a given probability under the method's assumptions, and intervals usually widen as the horizon grows.

Time-series cross-validation evaluates forecasts on a rolling origin: scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit keeps every training index before its test indices, with test_size, gap and max_train_size setting the test block, the samples dropped before it and the training window, whereas shuffled K-fold assumes independent samples.
AWS object storage, policy-based authorization, DNS naming and routing fulfill distinct request-path responsibilities.
Python dictionaries/lists hold local values; functions, exceptions, file context managers and JSON/CSV readers support explicit parsing.
Spark DataFrames use schemas and column expressions, SQL null semantics, lazy plans/actions and relational joins; formatted explain exposes a plan.

A Google service account is owned by the project named when it is created, which forms part of its email; the workspace service account has the form db-<workspace-id>@prod-gcp-<region>.iam.gserviceaccount.com; provisioning uses a customer service account added to the Databricks account console as an account admin and granted a custom Workspace Creator role; a cluster can carry a Google service account used for Cloud Storage and BigQuery; the service account with access to a customer-managed key exists within the Databricks control-plane project; a Compute Engine VM supports one attached service account whose tokens code on the VM reads through the metadata server.

For a customer-managed key on Databricks on Google Cloud, the service account with access to the Cloud KMS key exists within the Databricks control-plane project, and with the manual option Databricks does not use OAuth to grant it access; Databricks' reference architecture applies keys to managed services (notebooks, secrets and Databricks SQL query data) and to workspace storage (the two workspace storage buckets and GCE persistent disks), the storage key to classic workspaces only.

On AWS the Databricks network configuration takes at least two subnets in different availability zones with netmasks between /17 and /25 plus security groups, and a storage credential's IAM role requires a trust policy; Azure Databricks workspaces are Azure resources whose injected virtual network uses two subnets delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces with network security groups, with Private Link private endpoints for back-end, front-end and browser authentication, and storage credentials can use an Azure Databricks access connector's managed identity.

Private Google Access lets VMs in a subnet reach Google services without external IP addresses; a Cloud NAT gateway lets VMs in the chosen subnets reach the internet without external IP addresses; a VM without an access configuration has no external internet access; Databricks' examples enable Private Google Access on the node subnet, and Databricks' reference template creates no Cloud Router or Cloud NAT when back-end Private Service Connect is used.

Databricks' Unity Catalog guide for Google Cloud grants, for file events, a custom role with Pub/Sub topic and subscription permissions and storage.buckets.update to the storage credential's service account at project level, and roles/pubsub.publisher to the project's Cloud Storage service account.

Google Cloud firewall rules allow or deny ingress or egress for instances in a VPC network; direction defaults to ingress; priority runs from 0 to 65535 with 1000 as default, lower numbers take precedence and a deny beats an allow at equal priority; implied rules sit at priority 65535; target tags or target service accounts narrow a rule, and without them it applies to every instance in the network; the Databricks Workspace Creator role includes permission to read and create firewall rules, and Databricks' reference template creates an ingress rule for the Databricks subnet before the workspace and, when hardened without PSC, an egress rule using the region's control-plane IP addresses.

A front-end PSC endpoint, placed in a transit VPC, carries user connections to the Databricks web application, REST API and Databricks Connect API; private access settings choose ACCOUNT level, which admits VPC endpoints registered in the Databricks account, or ENDPOINT level, which admits only listed endpoint IDs; public_access_enabled defaults to true on Google Cloud and false on AWS, and with public access enabled an IP access list restricts public sources; the API description allows disabling public access only with both front-end and back-end private connections.

In Google Cloud's resource hierarchy the organization is the root node, folders organize an organization's resources and a project's parent is an organization or a folder; the IAM policies evaluated for a permission can include policies inherited from the organization, folder and project; organization policy constraints restrict resource configuration and are inherited down the hierarchy, where they can be overridden.

The Databricks Terraform provider documentation at v1.133.0 states that NCC binding is available for AWS and Azure only and in Public Preview on AWS, that NCC private endpoint rules are available on Azure and in Public Preview on AWS, and documents only AWS and Azure default and target rule types; the Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0 models a gcp_endpoint on NCC private endpoint rules with a target service attachment, Google API hostnames or all APIs that support VPC Service Controls; network policies list GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE as a storage destination type.

Back-end Private Service Connect for Databricks on Google Cloud uses two endpoints, one for the secure cluster connectivity relay and one for REST APIs; each is a forwarding rule in the customer's VPC whose target is a Databricks service attachment, registered in the Databricks account with its project, endpoint name and region and listed in the network configuration as dataplane_relay or rest_api; a workspace must be created with private access settings to support PSC scenarios; Databricks' reference template requires a customer-managed VPC and adds a private Cloud DNS zone for gcp.databricks.com, visible to the VPC, with records for the workspace URL, its dp- variant and tunnel.<region>.gcp.databricks.com; a PSC connection's status can be ACCEPTED, PENDING, REJECTED, CLOSED or NEEDS_ATTENTION.

A serverless workspace on Google Cloud is created with compute mode SERVERLESS and a region and needs no prerequisite resources; Databricks' reference template gives it no project container and no network configuration; the account API's storage modes are CUSTOMER_HOSTED and DEFAULT_STORAGE; classic workspaces report the effective compute mode HYBRID.

On Google Cloud a Unity Catalog storage credential creates a Databricks-managed service account whose email is granted access to buckets, and Databricks' Unity Catalog guide binds roles/storage.objectAdmin and roles/storage.legacyBucketReader on the bucket; an external location combines a gs:// path with a storage credential; with uniform bucket-level access only bucket-level or higher IAM policies control access; testIamPermissions reports the permissions the caller itself holds on a bucket.

A customer-managed VPC for a classic workspace on Google Cloud supplies a subnet in the workspace's region, with a netmask between /29 and /9, from whose range Compute Engine cluster nodes are allocated, and outbound access to the public network through Cloud NAT or a similar customer-managed appliance; one VPC can serve several workspaces but a subnet cannot be reused by other workspaces or resources; secondary pod and service ranges and the GKE configuration are deprecated and no longer supported.

A VPC Service Controls service perimeter describes a set of Google Cloud resources that exchange data freely among themselves; a request whose source is inside the perimeter and whose target is outside is blocked; the Databricks SDK's endpoint rule model includes an option covering all Google APIs that support VPC Service Controls.
